mcqs.question: Why is taking the whole system offline to reshard usually unacceptable at scale?
options: The downtime window grows with data size, turning into hours for terabytes of user-facing data
Databases physically cannot be copied while powered off
Regulations forbid ever taking a database offline for any reason
It would require deleting the old shards before creating new ones
mcqs.explanation: The core problem is that offline resharding time scales with data volume — fine for a small dataset, unacceptable when it stretches to hours for a production system. There's no physical copying restriction while powered off, no blanket regulation against downtime, and old shards don't need deletion first.

mcqs.question: Why does consistent hashing move far less data than plain `hash(key) % N` when a shard is added?
options: It only reassigns the keys in the small arc the new shard now owns, leaving all other key-to-shard assignments unchanged
It stores all data in a single shared cache, so no data ever needs to move
It compresses the data before moving it, shrinking the transfer size
It removes the need for a hash function entirely
mcqs.explanation: Consistent hashing's ring layout means adding a node only affects the small arc of keys nearest to it, unlike `% N` which reshuffles almost every key when N changes. It still uses a hash function and doesn't rely on a shared cache or compression to reduce data movement.

mcqs.question: A celebrity account's profile reads are overwhelming one shard, even though the overall keyspace is evenly balanced. Why doesn't adding more shards fix this?
options: Adding shards always fixes uneven load, so this scenario wouldn't actually occur
The hot key still lives on exactly one shard regardless of total shard count, so that shard's load doesn't change
More shards would make the problem worse by splitting the celebrity's data inconsistently
Celebrity accounts are always stored outside the normal sharding scheme
mcqs.explanation: Adding shards rebalances the overall keyspace, but one specific key still maps to one specific shard — a single hot key's load doesn't spread out just because there are more shards. This isn't a scenario that resolves itself, and celebrity accounts aren't stored specially by default.

mcqs.question: A team plans to reshard a multi-terabyte production database by scheduling downtime rather than building dual-write logic. What's the risk?
options: There's no real risk since a scheduled maintenance window is always safer than live changes
Dual-write logic is illegal to implement for financial systems
The scheduled outage can extend into an unscheduled one if a bug surfaces mid-migration, with no way to roll back live traffic gracefully
Scheduled downtime is always shorter than the equivalent live-resharding process
mcqs.explanation: A downtime window scales with data size and offers no graceful recovery path if something goes wrong mid-move, turning a planned outage into an open-ended one. Dual-write logic isn't illegal for any domain, and there's no general rule that scheduled downtime beats a live migration in duration.

mcqs.question: A 4TB dataset is evenly split across 4 shards using plain hash(key) % N. Roughly how much data needs to move when adding a 5th shard, compared to using consistent hashing instead?
options: Both approaches move roughly the same amount of data, about 800GB
Plain modulus hashing moves close to all 4TB, since the modulus change reshuffles nearly every key; consistent hashing moves only about 1/5, roughly 800GB
Plain modulus hashing moves nothing since only one shard was added; consistent hashing moves the full 4TB
Neither approach requires moving any data when adding a shard
mcqs.explanation: Changing the modulus in hash(key) % N reassigns nearly every key to a different shard, while consistent hashing only reassigns the arc the new shard claims, roughly total_data / new_shard_count. Both approaches genuinely move data, and the two costs are very different in scale, not equal.
